title: BehaveSim: Algorithm Similarity via Problem-Solving Behavior
one_liner: Measure whether two algorithms are truly different by watching what intermediate answers they generate while solving the same problem, not by comparing their code.
lead: When a language model writes a new algorithm, you cannot tell if it found a genuinely new idea or just rewrote the same logic in different code syntax. Two algorithms that choose nodes in opposite orders (closest vs. farthest) look nearly identical to code-comparison tools but solve problems in fundamentally different ways. This paper proposes a new way to measure algorithm similarity: instead of reading the code, run both algorithms on the same problem and compare the sequence of intermediate solutions they produce.

paras: When algorithms are written in code, traditional tools measure similarity by counting matching words in the code, comparing the structure of the code, or looking at the final answer. These tools have a fatal flaw: they ignore how an algorithm actually solves the problem.

Example 1: Two graph-search algorithms—breadth-first search and depth-first search—explore nodes in completely different orders and find different routes, but code-comparison tools rate them as similar because both use similar structures.
Example 2: The same algorithm written two ways (one using recursion, one using loops) should be identical, but code tools mark them as completely different.
Example 3: Sorting algorithms like insertion sort and bubble sort both produce sorted arrays, so comparing outputs gives no insight into their different strategies.

callout.html: Code similarity metrics measure surface details, not how an algorithm actually works.

steps.text: Execute algorithm 1 and algorithm 2 on the same input problem.
Capture every intermediate partial solution each algorithm generates along the way.
Assemble each intermediate solution into a sequence called a problem-solving trajectory.
Measure how different the two sequences are using sequence distance metrics.
Lower sequence distance means the algorithms solve problems the same way; higher means they differ.

paras: Instead of analyzing code syntax, BehaveSim compares the behavior of algorithms by looking at the actual intermediate solutions they produce while solving a problem. The metric shifts from static code analysis to dynamic behavioral observation.

hidden.name: problem-solving trajectory (sequence of intermediate solutions)
paras: A problem-solving trajectory is simply the sequence of answers an algorithm generates step-by-step as it solves a problem. For a sorting algorithm, it is the partial ordering at each step. For a graph search, it is the sequence of nodes visited. For an optimization method, it is the numerical values after each adjustment.

The paper compares two trajectories by measuring sequence similarity: low similarity means the algorithms took different paths or made different choices along the way; high similarity means they made the same moves in the same order.

heat.caption: Darker means more change in the intermediate solution. Highlights show where algorithms diverge most.

reads.html: Watch an algorithm solve a problem: you see it output an answer, then refine it, then refine it again. That sequence of refinements is its trajectory.
BehaveSim computes trajectory similarity using Longest Common Subsequence or edit distance on the sequence of intermediate states.

paras: Code metrics fail because two very different algorithms can be written with similar syntax, and two identical algorithms can be written in completely different ways. Trajectory comparison bypasses all of this by forcing both algorithms to actually solve the same problem and recording what they do.

When Algorithm A always picks the nearest unvisited node and Algorithm B always picks the farthest, both face the same graph, same starting point, and same goal. Their intermediate choices will be visibly different: Algorithm A's path stays clustered; Algorithm B's path jumps around. This behavioral difference shows up in the sequence of visited nodes, no matter how the code was written.

By recording these trajectories on many different test problems and comparing them, BehaveSim builds an accurate picture of how fundamentally different two algorithms really are. This gives LLM-based algorithm design a way to filter out mere syntactic variations and focus on genuinely new strategies.

stages.s: problem instance (graph, numbers to sort, optimization problem)
run algorithm A, record intermediate steps
run algorithm B, record intermediate steps
similarity score (low means different strategies, high means same strategy)

math.words: similarity score equals one minus the fraction of moves that differ when aligning two trajectories
symbols: the sequence of intermediate solutions from algorithm A
the sequence of intermediate solutions from algorithm B
the minimum number of steps to transform one sequence into the other
the length of the longer sequence

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Algorithm A visits cities in order: [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] (trajectory length 5)
Algorithm B visits cities in order: [1, 5, 4, 3, 2] (trajectory length 5)
Comparing position-by-position: positions 1 match (1=1), positions 2 differ (2 vs 5), 3 differ (3 vs 4), 4 differ (4 vs 3), 5 differ (5 vs 2)
Edit distance between these sequences = 4 changes needed to transform one into the other
Similarity score = 1 - (4 / 5) = 1 - 0.8 = 0.2 (very low, indicating fundamentally different strategies)

math.note: Lower scores indicate the algorithms explore a problem space in fundamentally different ways.

rows: Bubble sort vs. Insertion sort (final output match)
charts.note: All these tools give high similarity scores (94, 8 or 98) even when the algorithms solve problems completely differently.

charts.note: BehaveSim correctly assigns low scores when problem-solving behavior differs, high scores when behavior matches (regardless of code style).

items.b: Algorithms with similar code but different behavior may be incorrectly rated as different.
items.html: If the code is written in very different styles, the intermediate solutions might not align perfectly even if the overall strategy is the same. The metric requires executing both algorithms.

items.b: Algorithms that work on different problem sizes may generate trajectories of different lengths.
items.html: Edit distance between sequences of very different lengths requires padding or normalization; misaligned trajectories can give false dissimilarity scores.

items.b: Sampling only a few test problems may miss important behavioral differences.
items.html: An algorithm may behave identically to another on simple test cases but diverge on harder problems. Comprehensive evaluation requires diverse test instances.

items.b: Done right: run many test problems, align trajectories carefully, and interpret low similarity as a signal to inspect algorithms more closely.
items.html: The paper shows that on diverse algorithmic families (search, sorting, optimization), BehaveSim correctly clusters algorithms by their problem-solving strategies.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a simple graph-traversal problem (10 cities, Euclidean distances). Implement two algorithms: one that always picks the nearest unvisited node, one that always picks the farthest. Run both on the same five city configurations, recording the sequence of nodes visited in each run. Compute edit distance between the sequences. Show that BehaveSim assigns a low similarity score despite both algorithms being written in similar code, proving that the metric captures behavioral difference.
demo.metric_eq: sim = 1 - (sum of edits to transform trajectory_A into trajectory_B) / (length of longer trajectory)
demo.closing: The demo must show that two algorithms with opposite heuristics (nearest vs. farthest) receive low similarity scores, while the same algorithm written two different ways receives high similarity scores.
